new_statements.quote: Phonemic stress with a low functional load has been reported to occur in at least Yekora, Baruga, and Korafe. Examples from the Tafota dialect of Baruga from Farr and Farr (2004:10) follow. [...] The first form of each pair follows the default stress pattern apparent in the language and the latter of each pair deviates from it. [...] In the case of Proto Binandere, penultimate stress is assumed for two- and three-syllable words (at least in the case of non-verbs), based on the analyses of stress in the present-day languages; Suena, Zia, Binandere, Hunjara, Tafota Baruga, and Korafe all exhibit this pattern.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No source states a stress rule for Doghoro itself. The nearest published statement is Smallhorn's family-level summary: in the Baruga dialects (of which she treats Doghoro as one) and the other Binanderean languages the default is penultimate stress on non-verbs, with a small number of lexical exceptions that make stress marginally phonemic (Tafota Baruga 'aɣa 'coconut shell cup' vs a'ɣa 'thus'). The stress-marked Doghoro wordlist forms she reproduces (from Dutton 1968 and Farr, Pono & Umbefo 2000) are consistent with a penultimate default: 91 of 100 disyllables and 46 of 62 trisyllables carry the mark on the penult in my tally; the residue is mostly diphthong-bearing disyllables ('taima, 'maine) and a handful of final-stressed forms (do'mbu, e'mbo).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned for any Binanderean language.
new_statements.exceptions: Lexical minimal pairs in Tafota Baruga and Korafe ('phonemic stress with a low functional load'); verbs follow a different rule in Binandere and Korafe (stress on the first syllable of the tense/person/mood suffix, with exceptions in Korafe today's-past and some future forms). Nothing Doghoro-specific.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms in comparative wordlists; the statement is about Proto Binandere and the named daughter languages (Tafota Baruga is the closest to Doghoro), not about Doghoro by name.
new_statements.identity_note: Doghoro [dgx] / dogh1241 (alt. Dogoro; Dutton 1975: 119 speakers in two coastal villages, Bendorada and Sebaga, Dyke Ackland Bay; Smallhorn 2011: 270 speakers). Smallhorn 2011 (fn. 4 p. 2; §2.12 p. 54) treats it as 'essentially a dialect of Baruga' [bjz] / baru1269, kept separate only because speakers and SIL treat it as a language. The quoted stress statement concerns Tafota Baruga and other Binanderean languages, not Doghoro by name.
